Schünemann Graphics author: Carlos Cuello Last modified: 14 Aug 2025 Key message The PICO framework is an essential tool for developing clear and targeted questions for systematic reviews and guidelines. This framework is versatile, extending beyond management strategies to the evaluation of tests, prognosis, and exposure questions. Clearly selecting the target population, intervention and comparison of interest enhances evidence identification, synthesis, and analysis, ultimately facilitating the transition from evidence to decisions or recommendations. Review questions: looking for knowledge Questions about managements strategies The PICO framework is a well-accepted way to structure recommendation questions on management strategies. (1) It requires specifying the relevant population, the intervention of interest, the comparator(s), and the main outcomes. In this chapter, we will discuss how to sensibly choose the population, interventions, and comparators. How to select and rate the importance of outcomes will be discussed separately. The initial step that GRADE users typically follow when developing the PICO question is to select the relevant population. This population usually consists of individuals for whom the intervention is a practical and reasonable management strategy. Next, they carefully select and define the intervention of interest, which can include drugs, surgical and interventional procedures, diagnostic strategies, psychological, or educational interventions. One challenge with non-pharmacological interventions is the degree of specificity or description required. For example, “psychological support” for people with depression may be too broad, encompassing a range of clinically heterogeneous interventions that need to be addressed separately. Considering all types and modalities of psychological support in the same analysis can lead to unwanted inconsistency and inapplicability of the findings. Selecting an appropriate comparator is equally important. If a sub-optimal comparator is chosen or used incorrectly (e.g., regarding dosing or frequency of administration), it may result in an overestimation of the benefits of the intervention of interest. The selection of PICO components should ideally involve relevant stakeholders and experienced methodologists. They collaborate in an iterative process to identify and refine the components of the PICO question. Complex questions Sometimes, a new management strategy is considered as an alternative to the standard of care. In such cases, the recommendation question should compare these two options. Other times, the new intervention may serve as an add-on to the standard of care, requiring studies that compare the standard treatment with and without the new addition. Additionally, the new intervention might be part of a complex "package" of interventions, where one component depends on another. These packages can either replace an existing management strategy or be included as an add-on strategy. These examples are just the tip of the iceberg, as many combinations are possible. In order to frame sensible questions, both a deep knowledge of the content area and the methods used to study potential interventions are required, and thus framing the questions is a task that requires involvement of different stake holders and methodologists. Figure 1 – Simple and complex questions Another source of complexity can arise from the existence of multiple alternatives to an intervention. While a multiple intervention comparison framework and a statistical summary via network meta-analysis can help address this issue, it remains crucial to clearly define the population of interest and the interventions to be explored in the network meta-analysis. This clarity aids in interpreting the evidence, assessing its certainty, and making sensible decisions. Questions about tests In order to identify sensible questions about tests or tests strategies, it is important to clearly establish the role or purpose of a test or a test strategy. Tests can have different purposes; for example, they can be to diagnose diseases or conditions; alternatively, they can be used to identify important differences in baseline risk and prognosis of individuals; or they can be used for monitoring the treatment effect of an intervention. Questions about tests can be treated similarly to other management strategies, as the ultimate purpose of a test, regardless of its role in the healthcare process, is to contribute to improve patient outcomes. In this case the same components discussed before can be used to frame the question: a population of interest, the test-based intervention (or strategy), a comparison test intervention (or strategy), and the outcomes of interest. However, very often there is no direct evidence about the effects on relevant outcomes of different test or test strategies. In these cases, GRADE users may use evidence from diagnostic test accuracy studies to make inferences regarding the impact of using a test. These inferences may be done informally or through mathematical models. When the objective is to identify diagnostic test accuracy studies, the PICO framework can still be used, but it needs modifications: the intervention is replaced by the index test, and it is compared with a reference standard. Another particularity with tests is they are almost never used as a single intervention. Most often, tests are used as part of diagnostic pathways or strategies that lead to establish the approximate probability of a certain disease or condition. Also, tests can be combined with therapeutic interventions, and it may be difficult to estimate their contribution to the final health outcome. For example, the American Society of Hematology guideline panel addressed the following question: In a population with an intermediate clinical probability of lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, what is the optimal diagnostic strategy to evaluate them for suspected deep venous thrombosis? (2) Several combinations and sequences of clinical assessment, D-dimer and leg ultrasound are possible. Also, there is no randomized trials assessing any of the strategies. Thus, guideline methodologists used the data from test accuracy studies to model the proportion of false negatives (individuals with the disease but a negative test result) and false positives (individuals without the disease and a positive test result) of each potential diagnostic pathway. Then, the different alternatives were compared against pre-defined thresholds for the acceptable proportion of false negatives and false positives. These data, along with other considerations such as cost, feasibility, and access, finally determined the selection of one specific pathway over others and addressed the recommendation question. Additional review questions In guideline development and other decision-making processes, synthesizing multiple streams of evidence is essential for making fully informed decisions. One important aspect is understanding how individuals value the different health states resulting from the intervention of interest (relative value of outcomes). Additionally, it is often important to synthesize evidence related to resource utilization, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, and the impact on health equity. Integrating diverse sources of evidence allows decision-makers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the desirable and undesirable consequences of interventions. Each of these factors leads to specific review questions, which help identify, assess, and summarize the relevant evidence. These questions will be covered in more detail in the section on moving from evidence to decisions. Guideline questions: looking for actions Essentially, guidelines aim to balance the desirable and undesirable consequences of an intervention to decide whether it is an appropriate alternative for few, some, or most individuals. This complex question is subdivided in different criteria in the GRADE Evidence to Decision Framework to make the decision-making manageable, transparent, and systematic. From a high level, the Evidence to Decision Frameworks assesses: 1. The net health effect of the intervention (in relation to a comparison) and its uncertainty 2. The variability of individuals’ values or relative importance of the outcomes 3. Contextual factors such as resources, impact on health equity, accessibility, and feasibility Following the PICO framework, recommendation questions are typically framed as “in a population Z, should we use intervention X or Y? One key component of recommendation questions are the words “should” and “use”, although the latter can sometime be replaced by similar words (e.g., “offer”). Both reflect that guideline questions are about concrete actions. Practical advice It\'s very important to formulate guideline questions with specific and actionable focus. Take, for example, the question: "In patients with heart failure, should we investigate the precise cause using additional laboratory tests?" This question, while generally understandable, lacks clarity in its specifics. The absence of defined laboratory tests introduces two issues: firstly, it leaves the recommended action open to interpretation by readers, and secondly, it prevents the assessment of the recommendation\'s impact due to its vagueness. Consider another question: "Does Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) lead to cervical cancer?" This question, although relevant for understanding the mechanism of cervical cancer and the potential effectiveness of interventions like HPV vaccination, doesn\'t suggest a direct clinical action. This kind of question are often called "background question" that serves to inform the context of guidelines, rather than being the central focus. GRADE offers methods, tools and processes to assess the certainty of evidence and support healthcare decision making, particularly developing recommendations, enhancing the transparency in healthcare decision-making. It classifies evidence certainty ofto four categories (very low, low, moderate and high) based on study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and dissemination bias. The Summary of Findings (SoF) tables and Evidence Profiles (EP) facilitate evidence synthesis and communication while Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework supports structured decision-making. Introduction The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach offers a structured framework for assessing the certainty of evidence and supporting healthcare decision-making, especially in the development of recommendations. Its conceptual foundation supports a systematic, explicit and transparent process that defines the role of evidence, its certainty, and contextual factors in formulating recommendations and making decisions. GRADE acknowledges the need for judgments in this process. Rather than eliminating judgments or disagreements, GRADE enhances transparency by making these judgments and related deliberations explicit and structured (Table 1). It also ensures all interest-holders are contributing to those deliberations. Table 1. Merits of GRADE in comparison to other systems 1. Clear separation between certainty of evidence and strength of recommendations 2. Explicit and comprehensive criteria for rating down and rating up the certainty of evidence 3. Explicit consideration of the relative importance of various outcomes to patients and people 4. Structured framework and transparent process of moving from evidence to decisions 5. Explicit advice to make recommendations even when only very low certainty evidence is available 6. Clear and pragmatic interpretation of strong and conditional recommendations 7. Balance between simplicity and methodological soundness and comprehensiveness 8. Allows for adaptation and adoption of decision and recommendations (GRADE Adolopment) 9. Resources to learn about GRADE are widely available and freely accessible 10. Supported by an international network 11. Allows for innovation, refinement and further development 12. Supported by tools, e.g. GRADEpro Certainty of evidence GRADE defines certainty of the evidence as the "certainty that the true value of an estimate falls within a specific range or above or below a decision-making threshold". (1–3) The type of estimate for which certainty is assessed varies depending on the application of GRADE: in intervention questions, it refers to the treatment effects; when estimating patients’ values, it pertains to the relative importance of outcomes; in diagnostic questions, it may reflect the effect of a diagnostic strategy or, more commonly, the diagnostic accuracy measures of a test; in prognostic assessments, it typically represents a measure of association between a predictor and an outcome; and in environmental health and risk assessment, it generally describes the relationship between an exposure and an outcome. GRADE categorizes the certainty of the evidence as high, moderate, low or very low (Table 2). These certainty levels apply to the body of evidence assessed for each key question, rather than individual studies. However, some assessment (e.g. study limitation) are needed for each individual study in order to assess the certainty of the evidence. Central to the assessment of certainty of the evidence are two key concepts: decision thresholds and the target of the certainty rating. Decision thresholds are reference values that guide judgments about both the size of the effect (e.g., trivial, small, moderate, or large) and the associated certainty of evidence. Eventually they would also inform judgments of balance of effects of an alternative option relative to another (e.g., deciding whether benefits outweigh harms), or support commitment to an alternative (e.g., recommending one intervention over another). The target of the certainty rating refers to the specific range of interest (e.g., a moderate benefit) that is being assessed. It generally corresponds to the range or side of a threshold within which the point estimate falls. The certainty assessment is a 4-steps process: 1. Determining the number of thresholds: The first step in the assessment is to determine the number of decision thresholds that will be used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. The thresholds may be established through consensus or empirical evidence and should be reported transparently. 2. Determining target of certainty rating: The second step is identifying the target of the certainty rating, which typically corresponds to the range within which the point estimate lies. 3. Evaluation of the Evidence: In this step, GRADE users systematically assess potential concerns related to GRADE domains, such as study design and execution, including risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and dissemination bias. Dose effects and large effects may increase the certainty of the evidence. 4. Determining whether to Rate Down or Up: Identifying a potential concern in any GRADE domain does not, by itself, justify rating down the certainty of the evidence. Rating down is appropriate only when the concern introduces reasonable doubt that the true effect estimate may fall outside the target of the certainty rating. The same principle applies to rating up: simply recognizing a factor that might strengthen an inference is insufficient to increase certainty. An analysis is required to assess the potential for confounding or spurious results before rating up the certainty of evidence. Table 2 – Four levels for the certainty of evidence High certainty There is high confidence that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a specific range. Moderate certainty There is moderately confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate slightly from the target of the certainty rating (i.e. may possibly fall in a different range). Low certainty There is low confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate from the target of the certainty rating (i.e. likely fall in a different range). Very-Low certainty. There is very-low confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate significantly from target of the certainty rating (i.e. probably fall in a different range). Figure 1 – Interpretation of the levels of certainty of evidence for intervention effects. The figure illustrates the interpretation of the certainty of evidence on a moderate effect. Similar interpretations can be made for a large effect (e.g., the intervention results in a large reduction/increase), for a small effect (e.g., the intervention results in a slight reduction/increase) or for no important effect (the intervention results in no important difference). Certainty of the evidence about the effect of interventions For interventions, the starting point for rating the certainty of evidence is the study design, broadly separated into two types: • Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) • Non-randomized studies about intervention (NRSI) or observational studies (including but not limited to cohort studies, and case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, or case series and case reports). Although randomized controlled trials are the preferred source of evidence for assessing interventions, GRADE users often need to rely on non-randomized studies, particularly when evaluating potential harms, as well as the feasibility, barriers, and facilitators of implementation. Evidence from both RCTs and NRSI can be valuable, with each complementing the other. (4) In GRADE, a body of evidence from RCTs starts with a high-certainty rating, whereas evidence from NRSI typically begins with a low-certainty rating due to the inherent risk of confounding and selection bias associated with the lack of randomization. However, when a rigorous assessment tool, such as ROBINS-I, is used to systematically evaluate these biases, NRSI may start as high-certainty evidence. Nevertheless, such evaluations frequently reveal a moderate or high risk of confounding and selection bias, warranting rating down by two levels of the initial certainty. (5) Figure 2 – The GRADE approach for rating the certainty of interventions. The body of evidence of one or more studies will start as high or low certainty of evidence (CoE) if it is composed of randomized studies (RCTs) or non-randomized studies (NRSI) respectively (A and B). Five criteria can downgrade the CoE (C), and three will upgrade it when judged to be present (D). Based on these judgements a final CoE is obtained for the whole body of evidence for each outcome (E). If, from the outset, the evaluator uses ROBINS-I to assess the risk of bias of NRSI, the initial CoE should start as high (orange interrupted arrow) and then proceed to downgrade and/or upgrade as applicable using all GRADE criteria. Five domains can lower the certainty of the evidence from RCTs and NRSI These initial ratings are followed by detailed ratings across the five domains that can lower the certainty. The ratings are conducted initially at per outcome level. This requires detailed knowledge of the individual studies included in the body of evidence. In theory, each GRADE domain can justify rating down the certainty of evidence by one, two, or three levels. However, the criteria for rating by two or three levels have not been fully operationalized for domains other than imprecision. Limitation in study design and execution This domain evaluates the risk of bias arising from flaws in the design or implementation of individual studies. The primary method for assessing study limitations involves comparing studies with high risk and low of bias through sensitivity analyses, using statistical or graphical tools. However, there are scenarios where it may be necessary to rate down the certainty of the evidence, even when sensitivity analyses do not show any apparent differences. Three situations when this may be the case are: 1. when randomized is compromised (e.g., non-random sequence generation); 2. In unblinded studies, if investigator or outcome adjudicators can realistically affect the prognosis of participants or the measurement of the outcomes; and 3. If there is an important amount of missing outcome data and plausible assumptions change the effect estimate in relation with pre-stablished thresholds. Inconsistency This domain evaluates whether there are systematic differences across the study results included in an evidence synthesis. By definition, if only one study is available, there is no concern about inconsistency. (6) If inconsistency can be explained by a small number of a priori subgroup hypotheses, GRADE users may choose to stratify the evidence on the basis of these factors. However, if the inconsistency remains unexplained, the certainty of the evidence should be rated down. Statistical measures, such as I² and Cochran\'s p-value, provide an initial assessment of inconsistency. However, the final certainty judgment should be based on examining the effects of individual studies and their relationship with pre-established thresholds or ranges. Indirectness This domain covers concerns about applicability, generalizability, external validity, translatability and transferability of research results to a question of interest. GRADE distinguished population, interventions, comparisons and outcome indirectness in studies of interventions. A special type of indirectness (indirect comparison) results when two or more options are not directly compared within studies. The primary method for assessing indirectness involves comparing studies with more and less indirectness using statistical or graphical tools. However, there are scenarios where it may be necessary to rate down the certainty of the evidence, even when subgroup analyses do not show any apparent differences, for example when there are concerns about the baseline risk estimate. Imprecision This domain evaluates the risk of random error within a body of evidence. Confidence intervals around absolute estimates, such as risk differences or mean differences, are the primary tools used to assess imprecision. When these confidence intervals cross predetermined thresholds GRADE users should rate down the certainty of the evidence. (3) Additionally, even when large effects seem precise based on their confidence intervals, it is important to evaluate whether the evidence is sufficiently robust. This assessment depends on the total number of participants and events analyzed. If the effect estimates are based in a small number of participants or events, rating down due to imprecision may still be warranted. Dissemination bias This domain evaluates whether the accessibility of study results is determined by the nature of their findings. Although there are considerable challenges in judging the presence or absence of dissemination bias, the methods used in a systematic review, the characteristics of the body of evidence and certain statistical tools may be useful when judging its influence on the certainty of the evidence. Three domains can increase the certainty of the evidence of NRSI If, and only if, there is no reason for rating down the certainty of a body of evidence from NRSI, then upgrading the certainty of the evidence may be possible, within the following three domains . Large effect When a large effect is observed, the likelihood that this effect is entirely explained by confounding variables is very low. As a result, the inference of an important effect is strengthened, and the certainty of the evidence can be rated up by one or two levels. An important consideration is that when a large effect is observed, the target of the certainty rating will typically be set at a large benefit or harm. However, rating up the certainty does not imply greater confidence that the effect is actually large. Instead, it means that given the observed large effect, the probability that the true effect lies in the trivial or of no important range is very low. Dose-response gradient As with large effect, the presence of a dose-response gradient has long been recognized as supporting the causal nature of an association observed in NRSI. Such a gradient will often increase confidence in the findings of NRSI and thereby increase the certainty of the evidence. If a dose-response gradient is observed at the outcome level, the certainty of the evidence can be rated up by one level. (7) Opposite residual confounding Confounding variables generally tend to overestimate the magnitude of an association, thereby weakening the causal inference between an intervention and its outcome. However, in certain scenarios, plausible confounding may instead lead to an underestimation of the association’s magnitude. For example, patients treated in specialized centers often have a more severe disease compared to those treated in general centers. If better outcomes are observed in specialized centers, this finding is strengthened by the underlying difference in disease severity. Situations where the opposite direction of plausible confounding is at play are rare. However, when there is a strong rationale, GRADE users may consider rating up the certainty of the evidence by one level. Practical Advice When rigorous tools are used to assess the risk of confounding in non-randomized studies, the three domains considered for rating up the certainty of the evidence can also serve as additional indicators that the risk of confounding is moderate or low. In such cases, since the initial certainty is set at high certainty, the presence of any of these three conditions can justify not rating down the certainty or rating down by only one level instead of the default two. Overlap between GRADE domains Concerns or observations about a body of evidence may overlap across multiple domains. For example, in meta-analyses using random-effects model, confidence intervals reflect both within-study variance (imprecision) and across-study variance (inconsistency). Additionally, study limitations can contribute to inconsistency if results differ between studies with high and low risk of bias. Similarly, when a dose-response gradient is observed, focusing only on the extreme values may also suggest a large effect. A key principle in such cases is to avoid rating the certainty of evidence up or down twice for the same underlying issue. Certainty of the evidence about values Decisions in healthcare require not only evidence about the effects of interventions but also knowledge of the relative importance of the outcomes that interventions prevent or cause. This information can be obtained through a variety of means, including qualitative and quantitative primary research of patient values, qualitative evidence synthesis, or directly from patient representatives. Quantitative methods include the use of health utility ratings and can be used to express how important a health outcome is. Utility values can be obtained through direct methods (e.g., standard gamble) or indirect methods (e.g., quality of life questionnaires) and represent the average value individuals assign to a given outcome or health state. These values range from 0 to 1, where 0 reflects the value placed on avoiding death, and 1 represents perfect health. A related measure, the disutility (1 - utility), is often more intuitive. The higher the disutility, the greater the value individuals place on avoiding a particular outcome or health state. The certainty of studies reporting utility values start as high certainty evidence, but the same five domain used to lower the certainty of the evidence from RCTs and NRSI can be applied, although the operationalization is different. (8,9) Certainty of the evidence about the use of tests The best evidence about the benefit of using a diagnostic or screening test comes from RCTs of test and intervention strategies that directly measure the relevant outcomes. Indeed, if a test fails to improve outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy. (10) However, in many situations, direct evidence from intervention studies is lacking and the evidence from diagnostic test accuracy studies needs to be linked to other data to assess the likely effects on outcomes. This is a two-step process. In a first step, test accuracy studies are evaluated in systematic reviews, and where appropriate, combined in meta-analyses. The appropriate study design to measure test accuracy is observational, and the assessment of the certainty of the evidence therefore begins with a rating of high certainty. The evaluation follows the basic GRADE principles and the five domains for rating down certainty. (11,12) In a second step the best estimates of test accuracy are linked to other evidence, for example data on the prevalence of the condition, its natural history or the effectiveness of treatments. For recommendations based on linking different bodies of evidence, the overall certainty of the evidence involves an evaluation of which data are critical for decision-making. The overall rating is then based on the lowest certainty of any part of the evidence considered critical. Certainty of the evidence about prognosis and exposures Just as the GRADE approach is used to assess the effects of interventions, it can also be applied to questions about prognostic factors or exposures. In these cases, non-randomized studies are usually the most appropriate design and, unlike when used for interventions, they start as high-certainty evidence. The same five domains—risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias—are used to assess limitations in the body of evidence and may lead to rating down the certainty. (13) Evidence Profiles and Summary of Findings Tables To enhance communication and presentation of findings, the GRADE Working Group has developed standardized summary tables. The Summary of Findings (SoF) table is available in different formats to accommodate various needs. However, its core elements remain consistent, including outcome specifications, the relative effect of the intervention with its corresponding 95% confidence interval, an estimate of absolute effects, and the certainty of the evidence rating. The Evidence Profile (EP) provides similar information but offers a more detailed assessment of certainty domains. Like the SoF table, different formats are available to suit specific needs. (14,15) Additionally, GRADE has developed specialized SoF tables to present evidence on values, diagnostic test accuracy, prognosis, qualitative evidence and the effects of exposures. Developing recommendations and making decisions The GRADE working group has developed Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks in order to help guideline panels to use the available evidence and to develop decisions and recommendations in a structured and transparent way. (16) Guideline panels typically rely on multiple streams of evidence to formulate recommendations. Ideally, this evidence is gathered through systematic reviews, summarized within the Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework, and used to inform decisions and recommendations. At a high level, the default EtD template for interventions synthesizes evidence on the net effect of an intervention, the variability in values, and key contextual factors, including the FACE criteria: Feasibility, Acceptability, Cost, and Equity. More recently, a new version of the EtD framework has been developed to support decision-making based on evidence from multiple comparisons. For decisions involving one or multiple diagnostic tests, a specialized EtD framework is available. It clearly distinguishes between evidence on test accuracy and the potential impact of test use on patient-important outcomes. It is important to emphasize that the EtD framework is flexible and can be adapted to meet the specific needs of different organizations. Criteria deemed unimportant for a particular organization can be omitted, while additional custom criteria may be incorporated. For example, planetary health considerations may be included as an additional criterion when developing recommendations on animal food sources consumption or interventions that are associated with the release of greenhouse gases. Strength of the recommendations The strength of a recommendation reflects the overall balance between the desirable and undesirable consequences of implementing an intervention. GRADE distinguishes between five types of recommendations (Figure 3). Figure 3 – GRADE recommendations When there is high or moderate certainty evidence demonstrating a clear net benefit, a guideline panel may choose to issue a strong recommendation in favor of the intervention. Conversely, if high or moderate certainty evidence indicates a net harm, a strong recommendation against the intervention may be appropriate. However, such clear-cut situations are rare. More often, the net effect of an intervention is very small, variable or uncertain. For example, when the desirable and undesirable effects are closely balanced, the overall impact may be highly sensitive to assumptions about population or individual values. Additionally, when the certainty of the evidence is low or very low, effect estimates become unreliable, generating uncertainty about the net effect. In these scenarios, conditional recommendations are more appropriate. There are a few exceptions to this rule that are explained in one of the chapters. Those making recommendations or decisions should make all effort to provide a recommendation even if the evidence is of very low certainty because users of the recommendation are looking for answers that they will usually not have the time to explore with the same depth as a guideline developer or health technology assessment body. (17) Furthermore, the middle option of offering either alternative deserves special attention. It should be utilized for comparisons of two active alternatives when the choice between options is a sensible one. When the comparator is no active intervention of standard of care, choosing the middle option is not helpful for users of the recommendation. Offering to use an intervention or not is not providing guidance. Thus, users should choose this options when the intervention and comparator are really deemed equivalent. The GRADE Pro Software The GRADE process from creating a SoF table to interactive EtD frameworks and full guidelines is facilitated by the GRADEpro software (www.gradepro.org). GRADEpro is used by Cochrane systematic review authors to produce SoF Tables and by guideline developers to produce and publish recommendations online. GRADEpro can also be used to develop apps on handheld devices. Conclusions GRADE provides an approach to assess the certainty or quality of a body of evidence by outcome and across outcomes. GRADE also provides an approach to moving from evidence to a decision using EtD frameworks. The strength of the GRADE approach rests in the structured framework for the assessment of evidence independent of the actual intervention or question, and the requirement for explicit processes and transparent judgements. GRADE has been applied to a wide range of healthcare interventions, from clinical to public health and health policy questions. The ease of applying the GRADE approach will vary according to the type of evidence being assessed, the circumstances in which GRADE cannot be usefully applied are rare. The GRADE approach has evolved significantly since its inception in the early 2000s. Like any scientific methodology, it will continue to adapt to meet the evolving needs of decision-makers and to integrate emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence. Approval by the Guidance Group : Proposals undergo scrutiny by the GRADE Guidance Group, ensuring alignment with GWG objectives and preventing duplication of efforts. Inclusive Membership : Once approved, project groups are open to GWG members and newcomers, fostering diverse perspectives and expertise. Methodological development and approval The development process for official GRADE methods and processes that the GRADE Book is based on, involves six structured steps (see Figure 1): Problem Identification : Writing groups identify key challenges, drawing on real-world examples and brainstorming solutions through iterative feedback loops. Systematic or Scoping Review : If relevant, evidence is reviewed to identify existing methods and gaps. Where evidence is lacking, the group develops de novo approaches, ensuring that GRADE evolves to address unmet needs. Drafting : Initial drafts are prepared by the writing group, incorporating input from project meetings, expert consultations, and broader GWG discussions. Iterative Review : Drafts undergo multiple rounds of feedback from writing groups, project groups, and GWG members. This iterative process ensures clarity, relevance, and methodological rigor. Authorship adheres to ICMJE principles. Approval Process : Drafts are presented for discussion and approval at GWG meetings. Approval requires an 80% agreement, achieved through anonymous voting. Rejected drafts may undergo further refinement and resubmission (up to three times). Publication : Approved articles are finalized, peer-reviewed, and published in journals such as the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology and Annals of Internal Medicine and occasionally elsewhere . Concept articles may evolve into full guidance articles following additional field testing. Figure 1 - process for official GRADE Guidance and Concept Papers . GRADE concept and guidance papers are developed through a participatory, rigorous, and multi-stage process within the GRADE Working Group. All papers undergo external peer review, and authorship is determined in accordance with ICMJE criteria Ensuring quality and consensus Anonymous Voting : The approval process is designed to eliminate bias, with voting conducted anonymously to capture genuine agreement. Stakeholder Engagement : The inclusive approach invites input from novice and experienced members, ensuring comprehensive consideration of diverse perspectives. Iterative Feedback : Rejected articles are revisited and refined, with opportunities for resubmission fostering innovation and continuous improvement. Implications of the updated methods For interest holders Organizations claiming to use GRADE should align with the updated guidance and follow the minimal requirements for using GRADE, ensuring fidelity to its principles. Transparency in evidence assessment and decision-making processes is essential for maintaining the credibility and utility of GRADE-based recommendations and decisions. For methodological advancements The updated methods reflect GRADE’s adaptability, addressing evolving challenges in evidence synthesis and research methodology. By providing a rigorous yet flexible framework, GRADE remains relevant across diverse healthcare settings and decision-making contexts. For the GRADE and methods community The iterative and inclusive development process strengthens the GRADE community, encouraging collaboration and knowledge-sharing. It provides a platform for stakeholders to contribute to methodological advancements, fostering global alignment in healthcare decision-making. Conclusion The GRADE Working Group continues to refine its methods, ensuring that its guidance evolves to meet the needs of evidence synthesis and decision-making science. The structured, transparent, and inclusive approach to developing guidance articles exemplifies GRADE\'s commitment to excellence. By adhering to the updated criteria, stakeholders can confidently claim the use of GRADE, ensuring that their assessments and recommendations are systematic, transparent, and trustworthy. As GRADE evolves, its foundational principles — structure, inclusivity, and transparency —remain steadfast, ensuring that it continues to serve as a unifying framework for evidence synthesis and healthcare decision-making. The detailed description of its processes provides a roadmap for organizations and individuals aspiring to contribute to this dynamic field. Review questions: looking for knowledge Questions about managements strategies The PICO framework is a well-accepted way to structure recommendation questions on management strategies. (1) It requires specifying the relevant population, the intervention of interest, the comparator(s), and the main outcomes. In this chapter, we will discuss how to sensibly choose the population, interventions, and comparators. How to select and rate the importance of outcomes will be discussed separately. The initial step that GRADE users typically follow when developing the PICO question is to select the relevant population. This population usually consists of individuals for whom the intervention is a practical and reasonable management strategy. Next, they carefully select and define the intervention of interest, which can include drugs, surgical and interventional procedures, diagnostic strategies, psychological, or educational interventions. One challenge with non-pharmacological interventions is the degree of specificity or description required. For example, “psychological support” for people with depression may be too broad, encompassing a range of clinically heterogeneous interventions that need to be addressed separately. Considering all types and modalities of psychological support in the same analysis can lead to unwanted inconsistency and inapplicability of the findings. Selecting an appropriate comparator is equally important. If a sub-optimal comparator is chosen or used incorrectly (e.g., regarding dosing or frequency of administration), it may result in an overestimation of the benefits of the intervention of interest. The selection of PICO components should ideally involve relevant stakeholders and experienced methodologists. They collaborate in an iterative process to identify and refine the components of the PICO question. Complex questions Sometimes, a new management strategy is considered as an alternative to the standard of care. In such cases, the recommendation question should compare these two options. Other times, the new intervention may serve as an add-on to the standard of care, requiring studies that compare the standard treatment with and without the new addition. Additionally, the new intervention might be part of a complex "package" of interventions, where one component depends on another. These packages can either replace an existing management strategy or be included as an add-on strategy. These examples are just the tip of the iceberg, as many combinations are possible. In order to frame sensible questions, both a deep knowledge of the content area and the methods used to study potential interventions are required, and thus framing the questions is a task that requires involvement of different stake holders and methodologists. Figure 1 – Simple and complex questions Another source of complexity can arise from the existence of multiple alternatives to an intervention. While a multiple intervention comparison framework and a statistical summary via network meta-analysis can help address this issue, it remains crucial to clearly define the population of interest and the interventions to be explored in the network meta-analysis. This clarity aids in interpreting the evidence, assessing its certainty, and making sensible decisions. Questions about tests In order to identify sensible questions about tests or tests strategies, it is important to clearly establish the role or purpose of a test or a test strategy. Tests can have different purposes; for example, they can be to diagnose diseases or conditions; alternatively, they can be used to identify important differences in baseline risk and prognosis of individuals; or they can be used for monitoring the treatment effect of an intervention. Questions about tests can be treated similarly to other management strategies, as the ultimate purpose of a test, regardless of its role in the healthcare process, is to contribute to improve patient outcomes. In this case the same components discussed before can be used to frame the question: a population of interest, the test-based intervention (or strategy), a comparison test intervention (or strategy), and the outcomes of interest. However, very often there is no direct evidence about the effects on relevant outcomes of different test or test strategies. In these cases, GRADE users may use evidence from diagnostic test accuracy studies to make inferences regarding the impact of using a test. These inferences may be done informally or through mathematical models. When the objective is to identify diagnostic test accuracy studies, the PICO framework can still be used, but it needs modifications: the intervention is replaced by the index test, and it is compared with a reference standard. Another particularity with tests is they are almost never used as a single intervention. Most often, tests are used as part of diagnostic pathways or strategies that lead to establish the approximate probability of a certain disease or condition. Also, tests can be combined with therapeutic interventions, and it may be difficult to estimate their contribution to the final health outcome. For example, the American Society of Hematology guideline panel addressed the following question: In a population with an intermediate clinical probability of lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, what is the optimal diagnostic strategy to evaluate them for suspected deep venous thrombosis? (2) Several combinations and sequences of clinical assessment, D-dimer and leg ultrasound are possible. Also, there is no randomized trials assessing any of the strategies. Thus, guideline methodologists used the data from test accuracy studies to model the proportion of false negatives (individuals with the disease but a negative test result) and false positives (individuals without the disease and a positive test result) of each potential diagnostic pathway. Then, the different alternatives were compared against pre-defined thresholds for the acceptable proportion of false negatives and false positives. These data, along with other considerations such as cost, feasibility, and access, finally determined the selection of one specific pathway over others and addressed the recommendation question. Additional review questions In guideline development and other decision-making processes, synthesizing multiple streams of evidence is essential for making fully informed decisions. One important aspect is understanding how individuals value the different health states resulting from the intervention of interest (relative value of outcomes). Additionally, it is often important to synthesize evidence related to resource utilization, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, and the impact on health equity. Integrating diverse sources of evidence allows decision-makers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the desirable and undesirable consequences of interventions. Each of these factors leads to specific review questions, which help identify, assess, and summarize the relevant evidence. These questions will be covered in more detail in the section on moving from evidence to decisions. Guideline questions: looking for actions Essentially, guidelines aim to balance the desirable and undesirable consequences of an intervention to decide whether it is an appropriate alternative for few, some, or most individuals. This complex question is subdivided in different criteria in the GRADE Evidence to Decision Framework to make the decision-making manageable, transparent, and systematic. From a high level, the Evidence to Decision Frameworks assesses: 1. The net health effect of the intervention (in relation to a comparison) and its uncertainty 2. The variability of individuals’ values or relative importance of the outcomes 3. Contextual factors such as resources, impact on health equity, accessibility, and feasibility Following the PICO framework, recommendation questions are typically framed as “in a population Z, should we use intervention X or Y? One key component of recommendation questions are the words “should” and “use”, although the latter can sometime be replaced by similar words (e.g., “offer”). Both reflect that guideline questions are about concrete actions. Practical advice It\'s very important to formulate guideline questions with specific and actionable focus. Take, for example, the question: "In patients with heart failure, should we investigate the precise cause using additional laboratory tests?" This question, while generally understandable, lacks clarity in its specifics. The absence of defined laboratory tests introduces two issues: firstly, it leaves the recommended action open to interpretation by readers, and secondly, it prevents the assessment of the recommendation\'s impact due to its vagueness. Consider another question: "Does Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) lead to cervical cancer?" This question, although relevant for understanding the mechanism of cervical cancer and the potential effectiveness of interventions like HPV vaccination, doesn\'t suggest a direct clinical action. This kind of question are often called "background question" that serves to inform the context of guidelines, rather than being the central focus. Introduction The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach offers a structured framework for assessing the certainty of evidence and supporting healthcare decision-making, especially in the development of recommendations. Its conceptual foundation supports a systematic, explicit and transparent process that defines the role of evidence, its certainty, and contextual factors in formulating recommendations and making decisions. GRADE acknowledges the need for judgments in this process. Rather than eliminating judgments or disagreements, GRADE enhances transparency by making these judgments and related deliberations explicit and structured (Table 1). It also ensures all interest-holders are contributing to those deliberations. Table 1. Merits of GRADE in comparison to other systems 1. Clear separation between certainty of evidence and strength of recommendations 2. Explicit and comprehensive criteria for rating down and rating up the certainty of evidence 3. Explicit consideration of the relative importance of various outcomes to patients and people 4. Structured framework and transparent process of moving from evidence to decisions 5. Explicit advice to make recommendations even when only very low certainty evidence is available 6. Clear and pragmatic interpretation of strong and conditional recommendations 7. Balance between simplicity and methodological soundness and comprehensiveness 8. Allows for adaptation and adoption of decision and recommendations (GRADE Adolopment) 9. Resources to learn about GRADE are widely available and freely accessible 10. Supported by an international network 11. Allows for innovation, refinement and further development 12. Supported by tools, e.g. GRADEpro Certainty of evidence GRADE defines certainty of the evidence as the "certainty that the true value of an estimate falls within a specific range or above or below a decision-making threshold". (1–3) The type of estimate for which certainty is assessed varies depending on the application of GRADE: in intervention questions, it refers to the treatment effects; when estimating patients’ values, it pertains to the relative importance of outcomes; in diagnostic questions, it may reflect the effect of a diagnostic strategy or, more commonly, the diagnostic accuracy measures of a test; in prognostic assessments, it typically represents a measure of association between a predictor and an outcome; and in environmental health and risk assessment, it generally describes the relationship between an exposure and an outcome. GRADE categorizes the certainty of the evidence as high, moderate, low or very low (Table 2). These certainty levels apply to the body of evidence assessed for each key question, rather than individual studies. However, some assessment (e.g. study limitation) are needed for each individual study in order to assess the certainty of the evidence. Central to the assessment of certainty of the evidence are two key concepts: decision thresholds and the target of the certainty rating. Decision thresholds are reference values that guide judgments about both the size of the effect (e.g., trivial, small, moderate, or large) and the associated certainty of evidence. Eventually they would also inform judgments of balance of effects of an alternative option relative to another (e.g., deciding whether benefits outweigh harms), or support commitment to an alternative (e.g., recommending one intervention over another). The target of the certainty rating refers to the specific range of interest (e.g., a moderate benefit) that is being assessed. It generally corresponds to the range or side of a threshold within which the point estimate falls. The certainty assessment is a 4-steps process: 1. Determining the number of thresholds: The first step in the assessment is to determine the number of decision thresholds that will be used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. The thresholds may be established through consensus or empirical evidence and should be reported transparently. 2. Determining target of certainty rating: The second step is identifying the target of the certainty rating, which typically corresponds to the range within which the point estimate lies. 3. Evaluation of the Evidence: In this step, GRADE users systematically assess potential concerns related to GRADE domains, such as study design and execution, including risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and dissemination bias. Dose effects and large effects may increase the certainty of the evidence. 4. Determining whether to Rate Down or Up: Identifying a potential concern in any GRADE domain does not, by itself, justify rating down the certainty of the evidence. Rating down is appropriate only when the concern introduces reasonable doubt that the true effect estimate may fall outside the target of the certainty rating. The same principle applies to rating up: simply recognizing a factor that might strengthen an inference is insufficient to increase certainty. An analysis is required to assess the potential for confounding or spurious results before rating up the certainty of evidence. Table 2 – Four levels for the certainty of evidence High certainty There is high confidence that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a specific range. Moderate certainty There is moderately confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate slightly from the target of the certainty rating (i.e. may possibly fall in a different range). Low certainty There is low confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate from the target of the certainty rating (i.e. likely fall in a different range). Very-Low certainty. There is very-low confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate significantly from target of the certainty rating (i.e. probably fall in a different range). Figure 1 – Interpretation of the levels of certainty of evidence for intervention effects. The figure illustrates the interpretation of the certainty of evidence on a moderate effect. Similar interpretations can be made for a large effect (e.g., the intervention results in a large reduction/increase), for a small effect (e.g., the intervention results in a slight reduction/increase) or for no important effect (the intervention results in no important difference). Certainty of the evidence about the effect of interventions For interventions, the starting point for rating the certainty of evidence is the study design, broadly separated into two types: • Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) • Non-randomized studies about intervention (NRSI) or observational studies (including but not limited to cohort studies, and case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, or case series and case reports). Although randomized controlled trials are the preferred source of evidence for assessing interventions, GRADE users often need to rely on non-randomized studies, particularly when evaluating potential harms, as well as the feasibility, barriers, and facilitators of implementation. Evidence from both RCTs and NRSI can be valuable, with each complementing the other. (4) In GRADE, a body of evidence from RCTs starts with a high-certainty rating, whereas evidence from NRSI typically begins with a low-certainty rating due to the inherent risk of confounding and selection bias associated with the lack of randomization. However, when a rigorous assessment tool, such as ROBINS-I, is used to systematically evaluate these biases, NRSI may start as high-certainty evidence. Nevertheless, such evaluations frequently reveal a moderate or high risk of confounding and selection bias, warranting rating down by two levels of the initial certainty. (5) Figure 2 – The GRADE approach for rating the certainty of interventions. The body of evidence of one or more studies will start as high or low certainty of evidence (CoE) if it is composed of randomized studies (RCTs) or non-randomized studies (NRSI) respectively (A and B). Five criteria can downgrade the CoE (C), and three will upgrade it when judged to be present (D). Based on these judgements a final CoE is obtained for the whole body of evidence for each outcome (E). If, from the outset, the evaluator uses ROBINS-I to assess the risk of bias of NRSI, the initial CoE should start as high (orange interrupted arrow) and then proceed to downgrade and/or upgrade as applicable using all GRADE criteria. Five domains can lower the certainty of the evidence from RCTs and NRSI These initial ratings are followed by detailed ratings across the five domains that can lower the certainty. The ratings are conducted initially at per outcome level. This requires detailed knowledge of the individual studies included in the body of evidence. In theory, each GRADE domain can justify rating down the certainty of evidence by one, two, or three levels. However, the criteria for rating by two or three levels have not been fully operationalized for domains other than imprecision. Limitation in study design and execution This domain evaluates the risk of bias arising from flaws in the design or implementation of individual studies. The primary method for assessing study limitations involves comparing studies with high risk and low of bias through sensitivity analyses, using statistical or graphical tools. However, there are scenarios where it may be necessary to rate down the certainty of the evidence, even when sensitivity analyses do not show any apparent differences. Three situations when this may be the case are: 1. when randomized is compromised (e.g., non-random sequence generation); 2. In unblinded studies, if investigator or outcome adjudicators can realistically affect the prognosis of participants or the measurement of the outcomes; and 3. If there is an important amount of missing outcome data and plausible assumptions change the effect estimate in relation with pre-stablished thresholds. Inconsistency This domain evaluates whether there are systematic differences across the study results included in an evidence synthesis. By definition, if only one study is available, there is no concern about inconsistency. (6) If inconsistency can be explained by a small number of a priori subgroup hypotheses, GRADE users may choose to stratify the evidence on the basis of these factors. However, if the inconsistency remains unexplained, the certainty of the evidence should be rated down. Statistical measures, such as I² and Cochran\'s p-value, provide an initial assessment of inconsistency. However, the final certainty judgment should be based on examining the effects of individual studies and their relationship with pre-established thresholds or ranges. Indirectness This domain covers concerns about applicability, generalizability, external validity, translatability and transferability of research results to a question of interest. GRADE distinguished population, interventions, comparisons and outcome indirectness in studies of interventions. A special type of indirectness (indirect comparison) results when two or more options are not directly compared within studies. The primary method for assessing indirectness involves comparing studies with more and less indirectness using statistical or graphical tools. However, there are scenarios where it may be necessary to rate down the certainty of the evidence, even when subgroup analyses do not show any apparent differences, for example when there are concerns about the baseline risk estimate. Imprecision This domain evaluates the risk of random error within a body of evidence. Confidence intervals around absolute estimates, such as risk differences or mean differences, are the primary tools used to assess imprecision. When these confidence intervals cross predetermined thresholds GRADE users should rate down the certainty of the evidence. (3) Additionally, even when large effects seem precise based on their confidence intervals, it is important to evaluate whether the evidence is sufficiently robust. This assessment depends on the total number of participants and events analyzed. If the effect estimates are based in a small number of participants or events, rating down due to imprecision may still be warranted. Dissemination bias This domain evaluates whether the accessibility of study results is determined by the nature of their findings. Although there are considerable challenges in judging the presence or absence of dissemination bias, the methods used in a systematic review, the characteristics of the body of evidence and certain statistical tools may be useful when judging its influence on the certainty of the evidence. Three domains can increase the certainty of the evidence of NRSI If, and only if, there is no reason for rating down the certainty of a body of evidence from NRSI, then upgrading the certainty of the evidence may be possible, within the following three domains . Large effect When a large effect is observed, the likelihood that this effect is entirely explained by confounding variables is very low. As a result, the inference of an important effect is strengthened, and the certainty of the evidence can be rated up by one or two levels. An important consideration is that when a large effect is observed, the target of the certainty rating will typically be set at a large benefit or harm. However, rating up the certainty does not imply greater confidence that the effect is actually large. Instead, it means that given the observed large effect, the probability that the true effect lies in the trivial or of no important range is very low. Dose-response gradient As with large effect, the presence of a dose-response gradient has long been recognized as supporting the causal nature of an association observed in NRSI. Such a gradient will often increase confidence in the findings of NRSI and thereby increase the certainty of the evidence. If a dose-response gradient is observed at the outcome level, the certainty of the evidence can be rated up by one level. (7) Opposite residual confounding Confounding variables generally tend to overestimate the magnitude of an association, thereby weakening the causal inference between an intervention and its outcome. However, in certain scenarios, plausible confounding may instead lead to an underestimation of the association’s magnitude. For example, patients treated in specialized centers often have a more severe disease compared to those treated in general centers. If better outcomes are observed in specialized centers, this finding is strengthened by the underlying difference in disease severity. Situations where the opposite direction of plausible confounding is at play are rare. However, when there is a strong rationale, GRADE users may consider rating up the certainty of the evidence by one level. Practical Advice When rigorous tools are used to assess the risk of confounding in non-randomized studies, the three domains considered for rating up the certainty of the evidence can also serve as additional indicators that the risk of confounding is moderate or low. In such cases, since the initial certainty is set at high certainty, the presence of any of these three conditions can justify not rating down the certainty or rating down by only one level instead of the default two. Overlap between GRADE domains Concerns or observations about a body of evidence may overlap across multiple domains. For example, in meta-analyses using random-effects model, confidence intervals reflect both within-study variance (imprecision) and across-study variance (inconsistency). Additionally, study limitations can contribute to inconsistency if results differ between studies with high and low risk of bias. Similarly, when a dose-response gradient is observed, focusing only on the extreme values may also suggest a large effect. A key principle in such cases is to avoid rating the certainty of evidence up or down twice for the same underlying issue. Certainty of the evidence about values Decisions in healthcare require not only evidence about the effects of interventions but also knowledge of the relative importance of the outcomes that interventions prevent or cause. This information can be obtained through a variety of means, including qualitative and quantitative primary research of patient values, qualitative evidence synthesis, or directly from patient representatives. Quantitative methods include the use of health utility ratings and can be used to express how important a health outcome is. Utility values can be obtained through direct methods (e.g., standard gamble) or indirect methods (e.g., quality of life questionnaires) and represent the average value individuals assign to a given outcome or health state. These values range from 0 to 1, where 0 reflects the value placed on avoiding death, and 1 represents perfect health. A related measure, the disutility (1 - utility), is often more intuitive. The higher the disutility, the greater the value individuals place on avoiding a particular outcome or health state. The certainty of studies reporting utility values start as high certainty evidence, but the same five domain used to lower the certainty of the evidence from RCTs and NRSI can be applied, although the operationalization is different. (8,9) Certainty of the evidence about the use of tests The best evidence about the benefit of using a diagnostic or screening test comes from RCTs of test and intervention strategies that directly measure the relevant outcomes. Indeed, if a test fails to improve outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy. (10) However, in many situations, direct evidence from intervention studies is lacking and the evidence from diagnostic test accuracy studies needs to be linked to other data to assess the likely effects on outcomes. This is a two-step process. In a first step, test accuracy studies are evaluated in systematic reviews, and where appropriate, combined in meta-analyses. The appropriate study design to measure test accuracy is observational, and the assessment of the certainty of the evidence therefore begins with a rating of high certainty. The evaluation follows the basic GRADE principles and the five domains for rating down certainty. (11,12) In a second step the best estimates of test accuracy are linked to other evidence, for example data on the prevalence of the condition, its natural history or the effectiveness of treatments. For recommendations based on linking different bodies of evidence, the overall certainty of the evidence involves an evaluation of which data are critical for decision-making. The overall rating is then based on the lowest certainty of any part of the evidence considered critical. Certainty of the evidence about prognosis and exposures Just as the GRADE approach is used to assess the effects of interventions, it can also be applied to questions about prognostic factors or exposures. In these cases, non-randomized studies are usually the most appropriate design and, unlike when used for interventions, they start as high-certainty evidence. The same five domains—risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias—are used to assess limitations in the body of evidence and may lead to rating down the certainty. (13) Evidence Profiles and Summary of Findings Tables To enhance communication and presentation of findings, the GRADE Working Group has developed standardized summary tables. The Summary of Findings (SoF) table is available in different formats to accommodate various needs. However, its core elements remain consistent, including outcome specifications, the relative effect of the intervention with its corresponding 95% confidence interval, an estimate of absolute effects, and the certainty of the evidence rating. The Evidence Profile (EP) provides similar information but offers a more detailed assessment of certainty domains. Like the SoF table, different formats are available to suit specific needs. (14,15) Additionally, GRADE has developed specialized SoF tables to present evidence on values, diagnostic test accuracy, prognosis, qualitative evidence and the effects of exposures. Developing recommendations and making decisions The GRADE working group has developed Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks in order to help guideline panels to use the available evidence and to develop decisions and recommendations in a structured and transparent way. (16) Guideline panels typically rely on multiple streams of evidence to formulate recommendations. Ideally, this evidence is gathered through systematic reviews, summarized within the Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework, and used to inform decisions and recommendations. At a high level, the default EtD template for interventions synthesizes evidence on the net effect of an intervention, the variability in values, and key contextual factors, including the FACE criteria: Feasibility, Acceptability, Cost, and Equity. More recently, a new version of the EtD framework has been developed to support decision-making based on evidence from multiple comparisons. For decisions involving one or multiple diagnostic tests, a specialized EtD framework is available. It clearly distinguishes between evidence on test accuracy and the potential impact of test use on patient-important outcomes. It is important to emphasize that the EtD framework is flexible and can be adapted to meet the specific needs of different organizations. Criteria deemed unimportant for a particular organization can be omitted, while additional custom criteria may be incorporated. For example, planetary health considerations may be included as an additional criterion when developing recommendations on animal food sources consumption or interventions that are associated with the release of greenhouse gases. Strength of the recommendations The strength of a recommendation reflects the overall balance between the desirable and undesirable consequences of implementing an intervention. GRADE distinguishes between five types of recommendations (Figure 3). Figure 3 – GRADE recommendations When there is high or moderate certainty evidence demonstrating a clear net benefit, a guideline panel may choose to issue a strong recommendation in favor of the intervention. Conversely, if high or moderate certainty evidence indicates a net harm, a strong recommendation against the intervention may be appropriate. However, such clear-cut situations are rare. More often, the net effect of an intervention is very small, variable or uncertain. For example, when the desirable and undesirable effects are closely balanced, the overall impact may be highly sensitive to assumptions about population or individual values. Additionally, when the certainty of the evidence is low or very low, effect estimates become unreliable, generating uncertainty about the net effect. In these scenarios, conditional recommendations are more appropriate. There are a few exceptions to this rule that are explained in one of the chapters. Those making recommendations or decisions should make all effort to provide a recommendation even if the evidence is of very low certainty because users of the recommendation are looking for answers that they will usually not have the time to explore with the same depth as a guideline developer or health technology assessment body. (17) Furthermore, the middle option of offering either alternative deserves special attention. It should be utilized for comparisons of two active alternatives when the choice between options is a sensible one. When the comparator is no active intervention of standard of care, choosing the middle option is not helpful for users of the recommendation. Offering to use an intervention or not is not providing guidance. Thus, users should choose this options when the intervention and comparator are really deemed equivalent. The GRADE Pro Software The GRADE process from creating a SoF table to interactive EtD frameworks and full guidelines is facilitated by the GRADEpro software (www.gradepro.org). GRADEpro is used by Cochrane systematic review authors to produce SoF Tables and by guideline developers to produce and publish recommendations online. GRADEpro can also be used to develop apps on handheld devices. Conclusions GRADE provides an approach to assess the certainty or quality of a body of evidence by outcome and across outcomes. GRADE also provides an approach to moving from evidence to a decision using EtD frameworks. The strength of the GRADE approach rests in the structured framework for the assessment of evidence independent of the actual intervention or question, and the requirement for explicit processes and transparent judgements. GRADE has been applied to a wide range of healthcare interventions, from clinical to public health and health policy questions. The ease of applying the GRADE approach will vary according to the type of evidence being assessed, the circumstances in which GRADE cannot be usefully applied are rare. The GRADE approach has evolved significantly since its inception in the early 2000s. Like any scientific methodology, it will continue to adapt to meet the evolving needs of decision-makers and to integrate emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence.
